title: Jeremy Thomas, Legendary British Producer and Oscar Winner, Dies at 77
full_text: Sep 12, 2026 5:42am PT Jeremy Thomas, Legendary British Producer and Oscar Winner, Dies at 77 By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest Liam Neeson on the ‘Rage’ Behind ‘The Lost Children of Tuam’ and Turning Producer for First Time to Tell Story of Irish Scandal 18 minutes ago Maisie Williams Thriller ‘Ignition’ Bought by Saban for North America (EXCLUSIVE) 28 minutes ago New James Bond Movie: First Draft of the Script Is Done, Says Steven Knight 20 hours ago See All Getty Images for BFI Jeremy Thomas , one of the film industry’s most highly respected independent producers with a body of work spanning more than half a century, has died. He was 77 years old. Across his career, Thomas — who founded the Recorded Picture Company and later Hanway Films — helped bring to life more than 80 features, championing the work of both international cinema and daring auteur filmmakers in the process. Related Stories Bruno Dumont’s Cannes Movie 'Red Rocks' Sells to North America (EXCLUSIVE) Outsider Pictures Takes U.S. on Rafiki Fariala’s Award-Winning Cannes Hit 'Congo Boy' (EXCLUSIVE) Among numerous accolades and awards, Thomas won a best picture Oscar for Bernardo Bertolucci’s “The Last Emperor” in 1988. Popular on Variety Within his vast library of films, Thomas also produced Jonathan Glazer’s debut feature “Sexy Beast,” David Cronbenberg “Crash,” Christopher Hampton’s “A Dangerous Method” and Nagisa Oshima’s “Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence.” Other directors he collaborated with, many across multiple films, would include Jim Jarmusch, Takashi Miike, Werner Herzog, Terry Gilliam, Richard Linklater, Karel Reisz, Phillip Noyce, David Mackenzie, Jerzy Skolimowski, Ben Wheatley and Wim Wenders. Most recently, Thomas produced Herzog’s “Bucking Fastard,” starring Rooney and Kate Mara, which premiered at the Venice Film Festival last week. Meanwhile, at the current Toronto Film Festival, his latest collaboration with Miike,”Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo,” is due to world premiere on Sep 14. In 2006 Thomas received a European Film Award for Outstanding European Achievement in World Cinema. In 2021, Thomas came to Cannes as the subject of Mark Cousins’ documentary “The Storms of Jeremy Thomas,” recounting his numerous trips to the festival and work as a producer. He recently appeared in Luca Guadagnino’s documentary “Joie De Vivre,” which also premiered in Venice, about the cinema, art, and life of Bertolucci. The son of director Ralph Thomas (who directed many “Doctor” films) and nephew of Gerald Thomas (who directed all of the “Carry On” films), Thomas was born in London in 1949. He began working in the industry immediately after leaving school, helping in the cutting rooms for films including “The Harder They Come” and “Family Life,” eventually rising to edit Ken Loach’s 1973 TV short “A Misfortune.” While he originally wanted to be a director, Thomas shifted to producing, with his first producer credit being the 1976 feature “Mad Dog Morgan,” which he made in Australia for director Phillipe Mora. He later returned to the U.K. and produced Skolimowski’s 1978 horror “The Shout,” the first for his newly-launched Recorded Pictures Company banner. The film went to Cannes, where it competed for the Palme d’Or and won the Grand Prix de Jury prize. title: Liam Neeson on the ‘Rage’ Behind ‘The Lost Children of Tuam’ and Turning Producer for First Time to Tell Story of Irish Scandal
full_text: Sep 12, 2026 5:25am PT Liam Neeson on the ‘Rage’ Behind ‘The Lost Children of Tuam’ and Turning Producer for First Time to Tell Story of Irish Scandal Directed by Frank Berry, the powerful drama details the tireless work of local historian Catherine Corless that helped uncover a secret mass grave at a mother-and-baby home. By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest New James Bond Movie: First Draft of the Script Is Done, Says Steven Knight 20 hours ago ‘SNL U.K.’ Cast on Wanting ‘Bigger Swings and Some Sex Sketches’ in Season 2, Bloody Backstage Mishaps and if Jack Shep’s Princess Diana Will Return 21 hours ago ‘Everybody Wants to F— Me’ Director on Poking Satirical Fun at Performative, Arthouse-Loving Nice Guys and Casting Taron Egerton to Play One 1 day ago See All Liam Neeson was in his home in upstate New York in late 2017 when he was sent a link to a New York Times article about a shameful episode in Ireland’s history. Almost a decade on and he tells Variety he’s “still coming to terms with my reaction to it.” The piece, written by Dan Barry, laid bare the shocking revelations from a Catholic home for mothers and babies in County Galway on Ireland’s West Coast, where over the course of several decades until the early 1960s almost 800 infants and children had been buried in unmarked graves, unceremoniously dumped in a sewage tank and forgotten about. Related Stories Bruno Dumont’s Cannes Movie 'Red Rocks' Sells to North America (EXCLUSIVE) Wim-Wenders Produced 'I'll Be Gone in June' Bought for North America After Cannes Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) At the center of the article was Catherine Corless, an amateur local historian whose tireless dedication and unwavering sense of moral justice, often in the face of indifference (and, in the case of the Catholic Church, resistance), would help bring the appalling story to light. Corless’ work had already sparked national fury in Ireland, but Barry’s words would bring it to a wider, international audience, including one of the Emerald Isle’s most famous stars. Popular on Variety “There certainly was a growing rage, an embarrassment,” says Neeson on his first thoughts after reading the article. “I was brought up a Catholic. I was an altar boy for a bunch of years, and I was kind of staggered by it. And, for the first time in my professional life, I remember thinking: ‘Whatever my celebrity status is in this business, I want this story to be shown to more people.” So “viscerally struck” was Neeson that he decided to take a leap from his prolific on-screen career (he passed 100 film credits a few yearsa go) and turn producer for the first time, optioning the article for what would become “The Lost Children of Tuam” (the same name as the article), which now screens in Toronto having had its world premiere on home soil at the Galway Film Fleidh. “I just had to respond to it a some way,” he says. Directing from a script by Rebecca Lenkiewicz (“She Said”) is acclaimed Irish filmmaker Frank Berry , best known for “Michael Inside” and, more recently, “Aisha.” “When I saw those films, I thought — this is the man to tell this story,” says Neeson, who would also bring on board producers including frequent collaborator Jules Daly and Irish powerhouse Element Pictures. “Frank wonderfully eavesdrops with his camera and allows the story to breathe. And especially with this, you do not want to highlight the horror. You just let the story breathe, and the horror will reveal itself.” Frank Berry while filming ‘The Lost Children of Tuam’ Berry may have been brought onto the film a few years after Neeson acquired the rights to the article, but says he was instantly “aware of the immense responsibility” involved. “There’s a lot of people in Ireland and throughout the world who are affected by religious institutions, so that was on our minds every single step of the way. How would survivors feel when they’re watching this scene or when they’re listening to this dialog?,” he says. “But we started at the very beginning at the core of the of the film, which is this amazing character in Catherine Corliss, and we let Catherine lead us.” Speaking at “The Lost Children of Tuam” world premiere in Galway, where she was the star attraction, Corliss — portrayed by Monica Dolan in the film — told the audience about first hearing that Neeson was interested in speaking to her. “And she said she nearly fell off her chair,” says Berry. Neeson would eventually go to meet Corliss in her home (“I did not arrive by helicopter,” he notes). “And I had a wonderful afternoon just listening to her, assuring her this would come to the screen and for her to please exercise extraordinary patience,” he says. “I said: ‘Schindler’s List’ took over 10 years.'” “The Lost Children of Tuam” would take almost 8 1/2 years. But it was wait everyone was prepared to make to get it right. Much of the film was shot in on location in and around the town of Tuam itself — “it was very important for us to be authentic,” says Berry — where the director met a number of survivors of the home. Some of them would go on to appear as extras (Neeson says that, beyond a period where “it was in my head for about 10 seconds,” there was never any question about him starring on screen). “As with all my films, it’s really important to have lived experience at every part of the process,” says Berry. “It keeps conversations alive and fresh all the time.” Monica Dolan plays Catherine Corless in ‘The Lost Children of Tuam’ But it wasn’t just those who had connections to that particular home who were drawn to the project and wanted to get involved. “There’s so many religious institutions in Ireland that have hurt people, and that pain is is very, very palpable in Irish society,” says Berry. “From Mother and Baby Homes but also the secondary school system, even up into the 80s, and the Magdalene Laundries, which were open until the 90s.” As he notes: “There are survivors everywhere — and that’s why we made the film, and that’s why what Catherine’s doing, is so important. A lot of that pain is is hidden in Ireland and there’s a lot of wounds in Ireland that need air.” For Corless, her devotion to the story and her support for the film came with on core goal: to excavate the area around the home, to have the children reburied respectfully and for them to be remembered. “So this is this film is part of that journey, and that’s the goal she’s looking at. And she’ll rest when that happens,” says Berry. For Neeson, who asserts that “The Lost Children of Tuam” may be his solitary producer credit, he cites a a line from someone else to underline the importance of Corless’ work. “As the wonderful late Irish journalist, Con Houlihan, once said regarding mortality and memory, ‘to be forgotten is to die twice.'” Oscar Predictions: Supporting Actress — Is This the Year of Penélope Cruz? title: Maisie Williams Thriller ‘Ignition’ Bought by Saban for North America (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 12, 2026 5:15am PT Maisie Williams Thriller ‘Ignition’ Bought by Saban for North America (EXCLUSIVE) By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest Jeremy Thomas, Legendary British Producer and Oscar Winner, Dies at 77 3 minutes ago Liam Neeson on the ‘Rage’ Behind ‘The Lost Children of Tuam’ and Turning Producer for First Time to Tell Story of Irish Scandal 20 minutes ago Maisie Williams Thriller ‘Ignition’ Bought by Saban for North America (EXCLUSIVE) 30 minutes ago See All Maisie Williams in 'Ignition,' copyright NBF Studio 1. “Ignition,” the upcoming high-concept thriller led by Emmy-nominated “Game of Thrones” star Maisie Williams , has been acquired for North America. WestEnd Films — which launched the film in Cannes — has closed a domestic deal with Saban on the film, directed by Emmy-nominated filmmaker James Erskine (“Copa 71,” “Billie,” “Sachin: A Billion Dreams”). The deal comes following international sales including U.K. (Signature Entertainment), Spain (Twelve Oaks), Portugal (NOS), the Middle East (Falcon Films), CIS & Baltics (Arna Media), Eastern Europe and Israel (Forum Film). Related Stories Bruno Dumont’s Cannes Movie 'Red Rocks' Sells to North America (EXCLUSIVE) Outsider Pictures Takes U.S. on Rafiki Fariala’s Award-Winning Cannes Hit 'Congo Boy' (EXCLUSIVE) Currently in post-production, “Ignition” sees Williams — currently on screens in “Practical Magic 2” — play a woman whose drive to London is thrown into chaos when an anonymous caller informs her that a bomb has been planted in her car. Trapped and cut off from any outside help, she’s forced to follow the terrorist’s instructions, her every move watched, with no choice but to deliver the ticking bomb to its target — the Royal Albert Hall. As the clock counts down, she must use all her wits to survive and, as the synopsis describes, “uncover why she has been entangled in this elaborate terror plot.” Popular on Variety The film co-stars BAFTA nominee Rory Kinnear (“No Time to Die,” “The Diplomat”) and Lovi Poe (“Bad Man,” “Seasons”). “Ignition” — which was filmed using real locations and on live roads using remotely operated multi-camera systems — was produced by Victoria Gregory (“Maiden,” “Man on Wire”), Erskine, Sean Sorensen (“Black and Blue,” “Worth”), Adriel Thomas, Jason Maza (“Twist,” “10×10”) and Mark Stewart (“Heist,” “Escape Plan”). The deal was negotiated by Maya Amsellem, managing director at WestEnd Films, on behalf of the filmmakers, and Bill Bromiley, vice chairman of Saban Films. “Maisie’s performance leaves you on edge, brilliantly bringing to life James Erskine’s terrific script,” said Bromiley. “We are proud to be a part of it, and to be working with Maya and the team at WestEnd.” Added Maya Amsellem: “We’re delighted to have Saban on board for ‘Ignition.’ They immediately understood James’s bold vision and the film’s strong commercial potential. It’s a gripping thriller with a fantastic lead performance from Maisie, and we’re excited for North American audiences to experience it.” WestEnd, which acquired the film under WeLove, its label dedicated to promoting female-driven stories and championing female talent, will continue international sales at TIFF . “Ignition” was produced by New Black Films under its New Bright Films label, together with Playhouse Pictures, Sharp House and in association with Royal Viking Entertainment, Epic EV Studios, Vectorscope Films and C’est Lovi Productions. Executive producers include Williams, Michael Safai, Montgomery Blencowe, Jon Levin (“All The Empty Rooms”), Randy Jones Toll (“Roofman”), Steven J. Toll (“Roofman”), Ian Sharp and Pat Wintersgill. title: ‘On Behalf of My Son’ Director Gabriel Martins on Black Brazilian Representation in His Films: ‘It’s a Life Project To Me, Not Just Cinema’
full_text: Sep 12, 2026 5:01am PT ‘On Behalf of My Son’ Director Gabriel Martins on Black Brazilian Representation in His Films: ‘It’s a Life Project To Me, Not Just Cinema’ The powerful drama about guilt and reconciliation, having its world premiere at Toronto, is the biggest international hope this year from a Brazilian director By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest Toronto Premiere of ‘Le Faux Soir’ Crowns Great Year for Walloon Cinema, Built on Belgian Region’s Creative Freedom, Can Do Attitude 23 hours ago Ellen Burstyn Says Method Actors Today ‘Don’t Know Anything and Just Make a Lot of Noise’ 4 days ago ‘September 5’ Director Tim Fehlbaum Working on a ‘Historical Film’ Set in Berlin as Swiss Filmmakers Take on Challenges and Opportunities of Shooting in English 6 days ago See All Courtesy of Denise dos Santos/Netflix In 2022, Gabriel Martins made waves at the Sundance Film Festival with “Mars One,” a sprawling ensemble drama chronicling the life of a Black Brazilian family. At that time, the industry was still wrestling with what a post-pandemic future would look like and, despite “Mars One” having a strong festival run, Martins struggled to secure financing for his follow-up. Four years later, with Netflix on board, the director returns to a major festival with “ On Behalf of My Son ,” world premiering in the prestigious Platform section of the Toronto Film Festival , then heading to San Sebastián, where it plays in competition. Related Stories Bruno Dumont’s Cannes Movie 'Red Rocks' Sells to North America (EXCLUSIVE) Outsider Pictures Takes U.S. on Rafiki Fariala’s Award-Winning Cannes Hit 'Congo Boy' (EXCLUSIVE) The drama reunites Martins with Rejane Faria, who seesaws between the visceral and the poised in her embodiment of Vicentina, the mother of a bus driver who apparently killed himself and dozens of passengers in a planned suicide crash. As the woman begins to pull at the complicated threads that made up her son’s psyche on the days leading up to the accident, she decides to contact the victims’ families and apologize on behalf of Wesley. “On Behalf of My Son” is produced by Martins’ Filmes de Plástico for Netflix Brazil , and stars Maíra Azevedo, Renato Novaes, Karine Telles, Giovanna Heliodoro, Thalma de Freitas, and Grace Passô. Popular on Variety Speaking with Variety ahead of the film’s premiere in Toronto, Martins notes how “Mars One” came out at a time when “Brazilian cinema was trying to recover” not only from the impact of COVID-19 but also from the major budget cuts for culture and political instability under the Bolsonaro government. “This partnership with Netflix came at a very important moment,” he notes. “‘On Behalf of My Son’ was an older project than ‘Mars,’ a project I’ve tried to make possible for many years, but it was very complex,” he goes on. “We needed several locations, a large ensemble; the theme was dense… I think the film comes at a very opportune time. We were ready, as a production company, to make a film this big and make it the best it could be. Those were four years of maturing and making the most of all the doors ‘Mars One’ opened to us.” Having Netflix’s support gave Martins a much more robust budget and the possibility to deliver a film that remains intimate and heartfelt while also displaying a higher production value – including a memorable crash scene. “Netflix arrived as a partner at a time when the idea was already consolidated, and we had a very strong script,” he says of what the streamer thought of balancing the two. “What you see onscreen was already very clear to us, and they came into the project wanting to support this idea of working on a story that would challenge the audience but was also universal.” Higia Ikeda, director of films at Netflix Brazil, echoes that thought: “Netflix is proud to partner with visionary storytellers like Gabriel Martins. It’s amazing to see how such a particular Brazilian story can connect with audiences across different cultures.” “‘On Behalf of My Son’ is a true testament to how sophisticated and diverse Brazilian cinema has become,” she adds. “Through its reflection on grief, solitude, forgiveness, and how life’s encounters shape us, the film invites us all to appreciate the power of human connection. We’re proud to partner with a unique Brazilian production company like Filmes de Plástico to bring such a sensitive and powerful story to the world.” Courtesy of Denise dos Santos/Netflix But the film could have ten times its budget and still not work without a central performance as powerful as Faria’s, who is almost unrecognizable onscreen. The duo first met in 2013, when the actress was working with Maurílio Martins, one of the founding members of Filmes de Plástico, on the short film “Quinze.” “My understanding of cinema came from working with them. I left that film and made some more, learned some more, and eventually reunited with Gabriel in ‘Mars One’ and now ‘On Behalf of My Son.’” “Vicentina was a major challenge, something completely different from anything I had done before,” she adds. “Gabriel didn’t write the character for me, as I was too young for it when he wrote it, but since the film took a decade to get made, I inched a little closer to her in age, and our relationship also narrowed. He knew I could make it work and get her to the place he wanted. I gave all of myself to the role; I became a completely different person.” Faria credits the “trust” Martins had in her, as well as his sharp direction, with the success of her performance. “We achieved something great and very new when compared to the work we’ve done before. I had a great desire to see a different side of myself, and this character, who required a lot of makeup and had completely different body language, allowed me to step out of myself.” With “Mars One,” Martins became the first-ever Black director to be chosen by Brazil to represent the country at the Oscars. With “On Behalf of My Son,” the director once again brings a large Black ensemble to the screen, showcasing the strength of Black creatives in a country that still struggles with representation despite having the second-largest Black population in the world, and the largest outside of Africa. Martins cast the film himself, saying it is one of the things that “makes him the happiest” about the project. “I love watching these people; it was incredible to be on set with these people, and putting them in the spotlight is aggrandizing,” he continues. “It’s a life project, not just cinema to me. It’s a project that involves wanting to see a better world, and that goes through directing people’s gaze to these stories, to interesting people. It makes me want to shoot more and more. Arriving at such a major festival, a festival that has a lot of influence, with this cast, is a great life experience for me.” Faria emphasizes that working with such a diverse cast “becomes bigger than the film.” “To have the film play [in Toronto], to see the impact on everyone who’s involved makes me so happy, and amplifies the political aspect of it, too.” “The political comes alongside my well-being and that of all involved,” she goes on. “ We were very, very happy with how we made the film, and we yearned to have our peers with us. When Gabriel offers the opportunity of having a majorly Black ensemble, he turns a desire we have all had for so long into a real possibility: the desire not to walk alone. To not experience success alone, but to bring others with you. Opening these doors is so important. It is a major step, and it says a lot about not only what we have already achieved but what we are yet to achieve.” “On Behalf of My Son” will open in select cinemas in Brazil Nov. 5, arriving on Netflix globally Nov. 20. title: Carla Woodcock Joins Kate Beckinsale, Katherine McNamara in ‘White’ (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 12, 2026 5:00am From left: Katherine McNamara, Carla Woodcock, Kate Beckinsale Daniele Venturelli, Jemima Marriott, Araya Doheny Carla Woodcock (Starz’s Outlander ) has signed on to play the lead in White , the upcoming shark survival thriller from horror director Jake West ( Evil Aliens ), The Hollywood Reporter has learned exclusively. Woodcock will play Willa Harba, which the film’s press copy describes as “a struggling actress trying to catch her big break” who is traveling overseas for a shoot with a self-obsessed star when their private jet crashes into the Pacific. Willa is the sole survivor, stranded on a broken wing in the middle of the ocean with only a satellite phone to link her to the outside world. But when she calls her demanding studio boss (played by Kate Beckinsale ) for help, she brushes her off. Her signal gets picked up by a marine biologist Sam Swatek ( Katherine McNamara ), who has some bad news: Willa has crashed landed in the middle of White Shark Café, a stretch of ocean where great whites gather to feed. Related Stories Movies Canadian Auteur Matthew Rankin Had a Fever Dream About Canadian History Movies Almodóvar's Deep Dive Into ... Almodóvar West is directing White from a screenplay by Dan Schaffer, the writer and illustrator of the cult comic book series Dogwitch . Highland Film Group, which is co-financing White and handling world sales on the title at TIFF, has pre-sold multiple international territories, including to Splendid Film in Germany, IIF in Italy, Three Lines Pictures for Benelux, Cinemundo for Portugal, Falcon Films for the Middle East, Latin America to California Filmes and Rialto Distribution for Australia / New Zealand, among others. White is being produced by Yariv Lerner, Dominic Burns, Crawford Anderson-Dillon and Sky Morfopoulos. Kate Beckinsale is executive producing together with Highland Film Group’s Arianne Fraser and Delphine Perrier, Patrick Wintersgill, Kevin Glynn, Pauric Duffy and Hannah Leader. Highland Film Group’s current slate includes Nimród Antal’s sci-fi action thriller Bluefly with Russell Crowe and Priyanka Chopra Jonas; Neil Burger’s action thriller Barracuda starring Anthony Mackie and Dafne Keen; and Pierre Morel’s action thriller The Good Samaritan starring Daisy Ridley, Josh Duhamel and Sharlto Copley. Woodcock is repped by Sarah Camlett at Independent Talent Group. THR

title: How Meditation, Hope And Hard Work Brought Rosalind Eleazar Her “Long Shot” Dream Lead In Chris Rock’s ‘Misty Green’
full_text: Skip to main content By Baz Bamigboye Baz Bamigboye Columnist/International Editor At Large @BazBam More Stories By Baz How Meditation, Hope And Hard Work Brought Rosalind Eleazar Her “Long Shot” Dream Lead In Chris Rock’s ‘Misty Green’ Breaking Baz: Léa Seydoux Talks ‘Gentle Monster’s “Complexity” And “Contradictions” & Why She Wants To Take More Risks — Telluride Film Festival Kenneth Branagh Hosts Judi Dench, Anthony Hopkins, Ian McKellen, Gary Oldman & Helen Mirren In Telluride-Bound Doc ‘Into The Breach’ View All September 12, 2026 5:00am Rosalind Eleazar Stanley Morgan Slow Horses star Rosalind Eleazar says she fights hard for roles that “people don’t immediately assume I could play.” The latest example of this is her titular role in Misty Green , the new film from director-writer-producer Chris Rock , in which he also stars. Misty Green is a Hollywood actress who no longer has the town at her feet. A fast and loose substance abuse lifestyle has knocked her down from acclaim to disdain and forced her to beg for even minor auditions. Yet, Misty is like “a jaguar” — to use Eleazar’s term. She swirls around Los Angles with a swaggering brio that belies her penurious circumstances. Related Stories Reviews Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline's Reviews Reviews 'Girl Group' Review: Rebel Wilson's Musical Comedy Is Fun Spiritual Sequel To 'Pitch Perfect' -- Toronto Film Festival “If someone was to give you a breakdown of Misty Green I wonder if they would immediately go, ‘Rosalind Eleazar for that part?’” she tells me via Zoom from the Dolomites region of the Italian Alps. “I think people may associate me more with, I don’t know, something like being a lawyer,” she says. So Eleazar felt going after the role was “a long shot”, but she connected to Misty the moment she read Rock’s script. More importantly, she wanted the part. “It’s a dream role,” she says. Watch on Deadline Bigger names than hers were chasing it too. Having seen her work on stage and screen since the beginning of her career — which includes appearances on stage with the likes of Matthew Broderick and Ralph Fiennes; holding her own playing a memorable Yelena opposite Toby Jones, Richard Armitage, Aimee Lou Wood and Ciarán Hinds In Uncle Vanya at the Harold Pinter Theatre in the West End, and in The House of Bernarda Alba with Harriet Walter at the National Theatre and many TV films and series — Misty Green is undoubtedly the outstanding performance of her career, and by far one of the year’s best. The East-London-based actor admits “there were tears. I was crying when I thought I didn’t get it… As an actor, one thing I do share with Misty is that you go on this roller-coaster of emotions after you’ve auditioned and it’s out of your hands now, and the next day, you’re like, Oh, I think today I might get a call, and you just live in this endless hope. Then three days go by… So your emotions are constantly going like that,” she says. She’s in the Dolomites on a hiking holiday with her producer and actor husband Gabriel Lo Giudice ( The Wanderer: Destinations Unknown ) ahead of arriving in Toronto for TIFF , where she’s planning to meet up with Gary Oldman and some of the acting team behind the motley crew of Apple TV’s Slow Horses . Then, on Saturday, September 12th, comes Eleazar’s big night — Misty Green will have its world premiere at Roy Thompson Hall. Rosalind Eleazar in ‘Misty Green’ A24 Next month, the movie will have galas during the BFI London Film Festival and A24 will give Misty Green a limited release from October 9th. Daniel Kaluuya , Adam Driver, Anna Kendrick also star. Looking back over the whole auditioning process, Eleazar is incredulous over what she put herself through. Still waiting to hear whether or not she’d landed the role, she was in her London apartment “meditating, and I was trying to connect and talk to Chris in my mind,” she reflects with a rueful grimace then a smile. “At one point I genuinely thought I had connected to him, and then whilst I was on set, I said to Chris, ‘Do you remember? Did you ever at one point feel me talking to you?’ He just looked at me and went ‘ No ,’” she sheepishly divulges. ”You’re lucky if roles like Misty Green come once in a lifetime,” she says, “and I’m so happy that that somehow has worked out for me.” After two auditions over Zoom in London, the London Academy of Music & Dramatic Art graduate flew to Los Angeles for chemistry tests with Rock, who plays a director who understands that hidden beneath Misty’s armor of pain is an artist with proper talent. Once the part was hers, Eleazar sprang into action. She took singing lessons — performing “One Night Only” from Dreamgirls is one of the movie’s many highlights — and Rock tasked her with watching some movies, including Klute with Jane Fonda and Donald Sutherland. An aspect of Eleazar’s performance that fascinates me is the sultry physicality with which she infuses Misty. “I move very differently to Misty,” she says, explaining how the 5Rhythms method played a significant role in developing her walk for the movie. The 5Rhythms practice is a movement and dance practice created by Gabrielle Roth intended to liberate the mind and body. Eleazar played around with where she felt Misty’s natural tempo stood. Rosalind Eleazar. Photo: Will Aldersley “Obviously, throughout the day and through the course of whatever, her tempo changes,” she says, noting that Misty “has quite a lot of sexual energy to her.” The way Misty moves, Eleazar remarks, marks her as “someone that is also wanting to be noticed and someone that is wanting to be respected.” Eleazar broke out the Misty walk on the streets of LA. “It has to become like second nature, rather than something that on the day of film you suddenly feel self-conscious with because it’s not in your body,” she says. The street test helped her pare down the walk to what she describes as “a floaty staccato,” which allows Misty to “turn corners incredibly fast.” That means, Misty can catch you off guard, giving her a quite languid quality until she springs like the “jaguar” label Eleazar gave her. Eleazar, who studied Spanish, Mandarin and psychology at the U.K.’s Nottingham University, says she has “a lot of compassion generally for people that come out into the world punching and surviving, and they have these layers upon layers of protection because of whatever’s happened early on in their life, and they’re not immediately likable or lovable, and it takes time to love Misty. She’s not someone that you necessarily easily warm to.” Eleazar is generally drawn to larger-than-life characters, she says. In all her parts, from her Jacky Bast in Kenneth Lonergan’s 2017 television adaptation of Howards End onwards, she suggests there’s a commonality. “They’ve all been quite big in some way,” she says. “They’re eccentric and sort of Shakespearean, and I find that I enjoy looking for the humanity in those sort of larger-than-life characters.” Two days prior to auditioning with Rock in LA, she’d read with Ralph Fiennes in London for Rebecca Lenkiewicz’s play Small Hotel , which premiered at the Theatre Royal in Bath with Fiennes and Francesca Annis in the fall of 2025. There’s a slim chance of it transferring into the West End in 2027, if scheduling doesn’t get in the way. Rosalind Eleazar in ‘Small Hotel’ Marc Brenner For some reason Judi Dench becomes a topic in our conversation. When I remark that I still replay in my head the Cleopatra the great dame performed opposite Anthony Hopkins in Shakespeare’s Antony and Cleopatra at the National Theatre in 1987, Eleazar’s eyes light up. “Cleopatra is my dream role!” she cries. She’d love to play Medea and Elektra too. Surely working with Oldman, Saskia Reeves, Jack Lowden, Kristin Scott Thomas, Ruth Bradley, Christopher Chung, Aimee-Ffionn Edwards, Kadiff Kirwan and others on Slow Horses is like being in a theatrical repertory company, because they all come from theater backgrounds? Nodding admiringly, she says that the cast often takes tea with Oldman who “sort of watches over all of us and is interested in you and what you’re doing and is always a champion of your work.” She connected with Kaluuya in part because they both hail from the theater, although Misty Green is the first time they’ve worked together. “We would take lots of long walks together and discuss our shared history for the characters and also sharing our own stories. And he’s just an insane actor… I love dangerous actors — Anna [Kendrick] and Adam [Driver] too — you feel you can jump off together and see where you land,” she says, adding that her scenes with Kaluuya were incendiary. “Every take was so different and that beautiful trust you have with someone…” In the film, Rock’s character raises questions about racism and sexism in Hollywood but those subjects are not the film’s main concerns, a point that Eleazar concurs with. “Misty Green isn’t about race,” she says. However, she and Rock did have a conversation about it. “I think that there are places for different types of films, and this character was able to just exist, and there’s a universality to her. It didn’t matter that she was my skin color, that’s not the leading narrative of the film,” she says. And off screen whenever she has “potentially experienced certain things” related to race “I privately deal with it, and I kind of think to myself, well, let my work do the talking. I would love to be known as someone that is a solid actor rather than other things. But it doesn’t mean that I’m unaffected by it. Let’s say I’m not unaffected by sexism and racism in our industry,” she says. If Misty Green takes off for her the way I feel it will, then Eleazar’s going to be very busy. Could she move to Hollywood for work? She has an American passport. “I can I can work there if I started doing a lot more American projects and if it made sense. I do love living in London though, and still loads of shows are made out of the U.K. and in Europe.” Smiling, Eleazar looks directly at me and says: “This sounds incredibly cheesy, but when part of your dream is starting to become true, it’s actually also quite frightening, because you’re like, oh my gosh, I have portrayed this character in this movie, and I’m incredibly proud of all of our work. And it’s now at the stage of sharing with other people, and it feels exposing. But at the same time, I’m incredibly excited by it, and I’m feeling grateful. What an opportunity I had. And Chris giving me that opportunity — it was a long shot.” Misty Green will premiere 9.30pm, September 12th at Roy Thompson Hall at the Toronto Film Festival. ‘Practical Magic 2’ Conjuring $30M U.S.; NFL Week 1 To Impact Holdovers Company & State AGs Set Antitrust Suit Settlement Talks For October Noah Reid To Headline CBS’ ‘Sheriff Country’ Medical Spinoff, Will Guest On Cop Show ‘Onwards And Sideways’ Chat; ‘Girl Group’, ‘River’, ‘Stuffed’ Reviews; WB Chiefs Read More About: Comments

title: First Clip of ‘Club Kid’ Star Jordan Firstman as U.S. Voice Cast Lead in Cannes Breakout ‘Jim Queen’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 12, 2026 4:18am PT First Clip of ‘Club Kid’ Star Jordan Firstman as U.S. Voice Cast Lead in Cannes Breakout ‘Jim Queen’ (EXCLUSIVE) Global Constellation is screening the English-language version to North American buyers at TIFF By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest Hans Petter Moland Talks ‘Epic Love Story’ That Defined the Nation as Norway’s Oscar Submission ‘Growth of the Soil’ Debuts Trailer: ‘It Resonates with All of Us’ (EXCLUSIVE) 23 hours ago ‘Krux’ Director Tony Vahl Combines Practical Magic With Post-WWII Taboo: ‘A Belief Can Help You – or It Can Destroy You” 1 day ago ‘Viva Carmen’ Reveals Clip Featuring Singer Silvia Pérez Cruz – and Brand New Song – Ahead of North American Premiere at TIFF (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago See All Jordan Firstman, 'Jim Queen' Courtesy of Global Constellation Jordan Firstman , fresh off directorial debut “ Club Kid ” – acquired by A24 for release this November – leads the English-language voice cast of “ Jim Queen .” Variety reveals the exclusive first clip here: The animated comedy, directed by Marco Nguyen and Nicolas Athané, premiered at Cannes to rave reviews . Variety ’s Guy Lodge called it a “hilarious rare shot of broad comedy that plays like a queer ‘South Park’ on literal steroids.” Related Stories Outsider Pictures Takes U.S. on Rafiki Fariala’s Award-Winning Cannes Hit 'Congo Boy' (EXCLUSIVE) Bruno Dumont’s Cannes Movie 'Red Rocks' Sells to North America (EXCLUSIVE) “Club Kid,” which Firstman starred in, wrote and produced, also took Cannes by storm, sparking a bidding war . Popular on Variety He’s currently in production on Season 2 of the hit HBO series “I Love LA,” and has also starred in FX’s “English Teacher” and Mubi’s “Rotting in the Sun.” He’s represented by UTA, The Lede Company and Frankfurt Kurnit Klein & Selz. Firstman is joined by Mateo Lane , currently on his third international stand-up tour, “We Gotta Catch Up!” Most recently, Lane made his Broadway debut as Billy Flynn in “Chicago” at New York’s Ambassador Theatre, the longest-running American musical in Broadway history. Nicole Byer (“Nailed It!”), John Cameron Mitchell (“Hedwig and the Angry Inch”), Bob the Drag Queen (“We’re Here,” “RuPaul’s Drag Race”) and Wendie Malick (“Shrinking”) round out the cast. M’saada Nia and Wolfie Trausch lead casting and recording of the English language version of the film, while Moby and Lindsay Hick’s Little Walnut is producing the English-language version alongside Bobbypills. Global Constellation is privately screening the English-language version, featuring the U.S. voice cast, to North American buyers at TIFF over the weekend, as U.S. distribution rights are currently in negotiation. Following its buzzy Cannes premiere – which Thierry Frémaux hailed as “one of the most beautiful in the festival’s history in terms of atmosphere, comparable to what ‘The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert’ once was” – the film was released in French theaters by The Jokers Films on June 17, debuting at #3 at the box office – behind only “Toy Story 5” and “Backrooms.” To date, “Jim Queen” is edging close to 400,000 admissions and $3 million at the French box office, and is rolling out theatrically across more than 25 international territories in the months ahead. U.S. distribution rights remain available and are currently in negotiation. Produced by Bobbypills founder David Alric and Arthur Delabays, “Jim Queen” starts when Heterosis, a mysterious virus that turns gay men straight, sweeps through the Parisian gay scene. Jim, the six-packed sovereign of the Gym Queens, goes from Pride royalty to social outcast. With only Lucien, a freshly out twink with more heart than abs, still by his side, Jim must race to find a cure before the disease erases the community that once worshipped him. Co-written with Simon Balteaux and Brice Chevillard, “Jim Queen” is produced by Bobbypills, one of Europe’s leading adult animation studios. It’s behind James Gunn’s “Creature Commandos,” the first television series and first official chapter of the DC Universe, for DC Studios and Warner Bros. Animation. Its credits also include “Captain Laserhawk: A Blood Dragon Remix,” produced with Ubisoft Film & Television for Netflix, as well as the adult animated series “Crisis Jung” and “Vermin,” both streaming on Netflix. “Let’s face it – gay guys are obsessed with the way we look. It can be tough in this world, because you have to be in shape and you have to be young. I’m 43, and guys look at me differently,” Balteaux told Variety back in May . “I used to be a Gym Queen myself. Now, I’m going to be a Daddy. It’s the next step, so I’m making fun of myself too. Although I’ll still go to the gym tomorrow.” Nguyen added: “There’s a lot of toxic masculinity in the gay community, too. You think it’s enough to say you’re gay, only to realize you don’t fit the standards because you weigh too much. It was very liberating to write this, and to write these jokes, because we talked about what we’ve experienced.” Co-produced by Umedia (“The Count of Monte Cristo,” “Night of the Zoopocalypse”), it’s executive produced by Moby and Lindsay Hicks for Little Walnut in the U.S., and Katarzyna Janiak and Jacek Świgost for Timeless Studios, Arthur Cohen for Momentum Entertainment, and Fabien Westerhoff for Global Constellation. “I guess we made a political film, but it’s also because laughter can be a weapon,” said Balteaux. “We’re very lucky – we live in a country where ‘Jim Queen’ could be made. But we still think of those in Senegal and trans people, also in the U.S. Maybe it will lighten their reality a little.” Prime Video’s Stunning Drama ‘Sterling Point’ Elevates the YA Genre Beyond the Mundane: TV Review Octavia Spencer and Hannah Waddingham Are Badass Besties in Prime Video’s Middling Action Dramedy ‘Ride or Die’: TV Review Loading comments... title: Canadian Auteur Matthew Rankin Had a Fever Dream About Canadian History
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 12, 2026 4:00am Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney Toronto Film Festival Matthew Rankin’s films about Canadiana tend to have theatrical audiences rubbing their eyes. In his 2024 cinematic mashup Universal Language , marveling viewers could hardly believe a Canada onscreen where Persian and French are the two official languages and a local Tim Hortons becomes an Arabic tea lounge. With Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney — set for its world premiere on Sept. 15 as part of the Midnight Madness program at the Royal Alexandra Theatre in Toronto, Rankin’s genre-bending collage of archival footage, special effects and animation becomes a digital docufantasia of politics and pop culture, chronicling the journey to power for Canada’s 18th prime minister, Brian Mulroney. Related Stories Movies Sorry, Caleb Hearon Is Not Your Clown in 'Trash Mountain' Grief Dramedy Movies Courteney Cox Says She Decided to Direct 'Evil Genius' After Chance Encounter at the Beverly Hills Hotel: "I Made a Lot of Deals There" Rankin tells The Hollywood Reporter that his English- and French-language film looks to combine the two things his producer, the National Film Board of Canada, does best: documentary and animation. The result is a kaleidoscopic manipulation of moving images, backed by abstract language about the generational machinations of the then-Progressive Conservative Party over which Mulroney ultimately triumphed to become Canadian PM in 1984. “I don’t think of [the film] as a biopic. It’s the history of an image, how that image was created and how to mobilize his story to create a brand, to create a package that would ultimately become the brand of the Conservative Party,” Rankin explains. His fever dream of political maneuvering north of the border portrays ambitious men campaigning for power less as a series of contests by candidates seeking public office and more like TV wrestlers seizing the championship belt by unseating rivals after brutal title matches and aggressive storylines. “It’s like a blood sport,” the director says of the political environment that produced the joyfully combative Mulroney, who in one mixed-media collage wears a sequined and feathered robe like the ones boxers or professional wrestlers don to enter the competitive ring. ‘Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney’ Toronto Film Festival Behind the surface charm and inner furnace of ambition, Rankin portrays a Mulroney haunted by the early success of John Diefenbaker, Canada’s 13th prime minister, and the disembodied voice of Pierre Elliott Trudeau, another Canadian leader and father of the 23rd Canadian PM, Justin Trudeau. And as he won over Canadians, the director captures how Mulroney accomplished the Progressive Conservative dream: winning over Quebec, uniting a fragmented country and delivering economic gains coast to coast. “The Conservative Party is a bizarre coalition,” adds Rankin. “Mulroney had to unite disparate factions like disappointed Quebec separatists, Alberta rednecks and elderly ladies in Atlantic Canada, in addition to business leaders in Toronto and environmentalists on the West Coast.” The film also has a distinct parallel to today: the eventual fracturing of the Mulroney coalition led to the current Canadian political landscape, where Quebec and Alberta have separatist movements and the Conservative Party has moved further to the right than the former Progressive Conservatives. “The whole idea of the political center is more and more problematic, more and more tense, and this film does set a compass to where the center was 40 years ago,” Rankin argues. “Certainly, conservatism meant something very different in 1984 than it means in 2026. Donald Trump didn’t emerge out of the ether. There was a process at work, and it began then,” he adds. Rankin portrays that triumph over Canada’s political center ground by combining found footage with music and cultural elements because the director, like most Canadians back then, came to know Mulroney as a creature of TV. “He was the first to really create a sophisticated propaganda by seeing the potential in television and the packaging of his message in television. He really delivered,” Rankin insists. And to show Mulroney as the triumph of political performance over policy, the film blends archival footage, 16mm animation, pixilation and other experimental filmmaking techniques to play with vintage footage like analog-era TV commercials, political propaganda, as well as campaign buttons and brochures. In all, Rankin remixed and reimagined around 80,000 pieces of archival material to arrive at a portrait of Mulroney that is more video art installation than sober political biopic. ‘Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney’ Toronto Film Festival In one scene, Rankin offers an animated train steaming ahead with the giant brain of Diefenbaker as cargo, in an echo of fellow surreal Winnipeg director Guy Maddin and his use of brain models and motifs in films like Brand Upon the Brain! and Rumors . The director puts that satirical take on Canadian conservative politics down to his upbringing in Winnipeg. “The way I look at a thing, I always end up sort of seeing the thing and its opposite simultaneously,” Rankin explains. “Winnipeg is a very ironic place to live. It’s full of contradictions and hypocrisy and bizarre tensions, and when you live in a place like that, things become funny.” The same double vision extends to the film’s subtle nods toward current U.S.-Canada tensions: In archival footage, Diefenbaker is seen meeting U.S. President John F. Kennedy, while Rankin scrolls at the bottom of the screen “51st State?” while Diefenbaker, in a thought bubble, thinks, “Yankee go home.” Rankin’s visual layering and collage wastes little time in showing Diefenbaker and other Conservative Party politicians falling out of favor with Canadians, only for Irish Catholic Mulroney — famed for singing “When Irish Eyes Are Smiling” off-key — to emerge from the wings and win power in an eventual landslide, at a time when like-minded conservatives like Margaret Thatcher led Britain as prime minister and Ronald Reagan sat in the White House as the U.S. president. In the end, Rankin’s Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney chooses neither a hagiography or a curb-stomping critique, instead portraying an ambitious, risk-taking politician who managed to charm Canadians until he fell out of favor at the ballot box. For Rankin, the moral murkiness is the point. “I feel when we see Mulroney being kind of duplicitous or ruthless or superficial or whatever, these things that are typically lobbed at him honestly make me like him a little bit more.” THR

title: ‘Dau’ Review: Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s Vast Cinematic Experiment in Historical World-Building Remains More Impressive From a Distance
full_text: Sep 12, 2026 3:49am PT ‘Dau’ Review: Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s Vast Cinematic Experiment in Historical World-Building Remains More Impressive From a Distance The heftiest feature film to emerge so far from the 20-year multidisciplinary DAU project follows four decades in the life of a Greek-born physicist at odds with the Soviet state. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘Dau’ Review: Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s Vast Cinematic Experiment in Historical World-Building Remains More Impressive From a Distance 2 hours ago ‘Stuffed’ Review: Jodie Comer and Harry Melling Sing the Body Eccentric in an Odd, and Oddly Touching, Taxidermy Musical 2 days ago ‘Company’ Review: Casey Affleck’s Latest Directorial Effort Isn’t What It Initially Appears to Be, but Isn’t Very Interesting Either Way 3 days ago See All Venice Film Festival More than six years after Ilya Khrzhanovsky premiered “ DAU . Natasha” and “DAU. Degeneration” at the Berlin Film Festival — right before the global COVID lockdown — to a politely muted reception and limited distributor interest, you might think the moment has passed for another missive from the DAU Cinematic Universe. Turns out, however, that you can’t keep a good immersive multidisciplinary art project dau. Or even a flawed and ethically questionable one: Allegations of physical and psychological abuse on the sprawling set of this years-long undertaking have surfaced prominently, but not enough to deter the Venice Film Festival from programming “Dau” — seemingly, as implied by the back-to-basics title, Khrzhanovsky’s attempt to extract a quintessential dramatic epic from untold reams of material — in its main competition. Related Stories Bruno Dumont’s Cannes Movie 'Red Rocks' Sells to North America (EXCLUSIVE) Outsider Pictures Takes U.S. on Rafiki Fariala’s Award-Winning Cannes Hit 'Congo Boy' (EXCLUSIVE) The ethics of that decision are further fodder for debate, though festival brass have defended the film on political grounds. Certainly, you can argue that Khrzhanovsky’s overarching thesis, with its heavy focus on the grim tools of Russian state oppression and imperialism through history, has gained in timeliness since we last checked in on the DAU project, before Putin’s invasion of Ukraine. The other question to ask, however, is whether “Dau” is such an undeniable artistic accomplishment as to merit all this back and forth — and on that, the jury is out. Popular on Variety Weighing in at just over 200 minutes (not including the quarter-hour interval bisecting its Venice presentation), and spanning four decades in the life of a physicist involved in the Soviet atom-bomb project, the film certainly announces itself as a grave and major work. But beneath the impressive, sometimes seizure-threatening sound and fury of its formal construction, “Dau” feels dramatically and rhetorically thin: It plays as an avant-garde counterpart to such American films as “Oppenheimer” and “The Brutalist” (whose Oscar-winning DP, Lol Crawley, is one of three credited here), which likewise portrayed the social and ideological turmoil of a historical era through the portrait of a single tortured man. The man in this case remains something of a cypher to the last. The character is inspired by Lev Landau, a leading Soviet theoretical physicist who won a Nobel Prize in 1962, and whose achievements included calculating the dynamics of the first Soviet thermonuclear bomb. Landau’s own life story is eventual enough to sustain a conventional biopic, though of course “conventional” is not part of Khrzhanovsky’s mission. The film’s fictionalized protagonist, known only as Dau, is Greek-born, and played with gangly, wild-eyed physicality by the Greek-Russian musician Teodor Currentzis — whether or not Dau’s nationality was dictated by the casting, we never really learn the backstory of what brought him to the Soviet Union. He is, however, effectively marked as an outsider from the off, beginning with his eccentric appearance and dress — for the first half of the film’s extensive timeline, he’s consistently clad in glaring red velvet against the sober neutrals of the men around him. He’s introduced in 1928, striding with purpose down the heaving, filthy, vermin-infested streets of Leningrad in a grimily kaleidoscopic sequence barely tamed from the dizzily cacophonous montage of disconnected imagery — bodies, blackboard calculations, archival shreds of war and strife — that begins (and bookends) the film. It’s a vivid establishment of time and place, but we immediately lurch forward to mid-1930s Kharkiv, where we get better acquainted with Dau as a young rebel scientist thumbing his nose at the military industry that would like to employ him — arguing to his uniformed would-be recruiters that the job of the physicist is to discover new spaces, not defend existing territories. It’s the kind of principled stance that can only be beaten out of him by the state, but there’s plenty of time for that yet. The Kharkiv years also see him meet young working-class woman Nora (Radmila Shegoleva), cuing a marriage that will also be significantly corrupted in the hours to come. In the late 1930s, facing a choice between cooperation or consignment to a penal colony, he’s finally absorbed into a state scientific research institute in Moscow, where the rest of the film bitterly unfolds — a semi-surreal, oppressively over-scaled place that steadily consumes his mind, his principles and his freedom, under the unforgiving surveillance of government interrogator Azhippo (Vladimir Azhippo). What release he can find comes via a parade of extramarital affairs that progressively darken the mood of his domestic life — a holding pattern of misery that indeed holds through the film’s second half. Rather than opening up as a character, Dau recedes from us as time ticks by: His gradual ruin illuminates little that the film hasn’t already made obvious about the living nightmare of this milieu. Compensation come in a proliferation of visually and sonically startling setpieces that mostly serve to show off the unhinged dedication of the DAU project’s literal world-building. One fairly ordinary dialogue scene takes place atop an expansive steel grate suspended in mid-air; another at the foot of a gargantuan state sculpture surrounded by extras walking, for reasons unknown, at a perfect 45-degree angle; when Dau is violently attacked in the street, it’s against a mountain of cabbages scaled and loudly peeled by oblivious scavengers. As a sheer feat of production design and crowd choreography, then, “Dau” is occasionally jaw-dropping, though it still offers only a glimpse of the huge, mad artistic and practical undertaking that DAU is — conceived as a kind of quasi-“Truman Show”-style experiment in which participants lived and worked full-time on a 24/7 set spanning 12,000 square meters. None of the fictional DAU films set within this colossal recreation can be as interesting as the wider view, and “Dau,” for all its grandiose ambition, is no exception. Khrzhanovsky himself has described the films as mere trailers for the larger project; it would take a more hybrid form of cinema to capture the scope and folly of what has been achieved. ‘Dau’ Review: Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s Vast Cinematic Experiment in Historical World-Building Remains More Impressive From a Distance Reviewed at Venice Film Festival (Competition), Sept. 6, 2026. Running time: 202 MIN. Production: (Germany-France-Sweden) A Phenomen Berlin Filmproduktions, Essential Films, Société Parisienne de Production, Plattform Produktion production. (World sales: Producers: Ilya Khrzhanovsky, Philippe Bober, Leonid Lebedev. Co-producers: Susanne Mariann, Solal Coutard, Svetlana Dragayeva, Erik Hemmendorf. Crew: Director: Ilya Khrzhanovsky. Screenplay: Khrzhanovsky, with Susanne Marian, Vladimir Sorokin, Ilia Permiakov. Camera: Jürgen Jürges, Manuel Alberto Claro, Lol Crawley. Editors: Ilia Permiakov, Rob Myers. With: Teodor Currentzis, Radmila Shegoleva, Anatoly Vasiliev, Vladimir Azhippo, Dmitri Tcherniakov, Dmitry Cheglakov, Demyan Kudryavtsev, Maria Nafpliotou, Ekaterina Andreeva, Victoriia Skytska, Konstantin Leshan, Ekaterina Pachkovskaya, Alexey Blinov, Aleksey Trifonov, Peteris Kimelis, Nikita Nekrasov, Alexander Migdal, David Gross, Carlo Rovelli, James Fallon, Peter Sellars, Daniil Ishmatov, Yuriy Alekseev, Pavel Gordienko, Vladimir Yermolenko, Nikolay Voronov, Carsten Höller, Marina Abramović, Romeo Castellucci. title: ‘Totém’ Director Lila Avilés Wraps Production on ‘Cábula,’ Releases First Look (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 12, 2026 3:40am PT ‘Totém’ Director Lila Avilés Wraps Production on ‘Cábula,’ Releases First Look (EXCLUSIVE) By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest ‘Totém’ Director Lila Avilés Wraps Production on ‘Cábula,’ Releases First Look (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Global Africa Hub at TIFF Market Seeks to Boost Visibility — and Deals — for African Filmmakers in Toronto: ‘It’s Our Moment’ 24 hours ago Telekom Srbija’s Content Head on Blueprint for Turning Serbian Production Powerhouse Into Global Player 2 days ago See All Courtesy Cuadernos de Cine Mexican filmmaker Lila Avilés (“Totém”) has wrapped production on her next feature film, “Cábula,” and shared an exclusive first-look image with Variety. The director presented the film during the Venice Gap-Financing Market , which took place from Sept. 4 – 6. Set in the fictional Mexican town of Mexicalpan, “Cábula” follows Toña, a dedicated and deeply compassionate teacher who is committed to nurturing her students’ creativity. When an invitation to represent their community takes Toña and her class to the capital, they encounter an absurd group of elites determined to appropriate and exploit their customs. But despite a series of challenges and betrayals, Toña reaffirms her calling and her belief in the transformative power of education. Related Stories Bruno Dumont’s Cannes Movie 'Red Rocks' Sells to North America (EXCLUSIVE) Outsider Pictures Takes U.S. on Rafiki Fariala’s Award-Winning Cannes Hit 'Congo Boy' (EXCLUSIVE) Written by Avilés and Miguel Vasallo, “Cábula” is produced by Nicolás Celis (one of the producers of multi-Oscar winner “Roma”) for Cuadernos de Cine, the Mexico City-based shingle founded by Celis in 2008 and a sister company to production powerhouse Pimienta Films. It’s co-produced by Maria Zamora of Elastica Films and stars Teresita Sánchez, Gabriela Cartol and Montserrat Marañón. Popular on Variety The film marks Avilés’ long-awaited follow-up to “Totém,” which wowed audiences as well as the jurors at the 2023 Berlinale, where it won the Ecumenical Prize. Variety ’s Peter Debruge praised the “intimate, emotionally rich” drama, singling out the director’s “generous, open-ended style” in what he described as a “multilayered follow-up to ‘The Chambermaid.’” That film, which marked Avilés’ auspicious debut, premiered at the Toronto Film Festival in 2018, where it won the Ariel First Feature Film Award. According to a director’s statement provided to Variety , Avilés’ latest “uses comedy as resistance against a cruel, dehumanizing world… [and] explores humor as an escape valve and a collective mirror to question power, rebuilding the social fabric through vulnerability, tenderness and irreverence. At its heart is a tribute to education. In a country of minimal budgets, underpaid teachers become anonymous heroes.” Utilizing a mix of seasoned professional actors and fresh local talents, “Cábula” stars Teresita Sánchez, the veteran Mexican actress who featured in both “The Chambermaid” and “Totém.” Speaking to Variety from Mexico City, Avilés referred to Sánchez as her “muse,” comparing her to Federico Fellini’s wife, Giulietta Messina. “She has that energy that can make you cry, can make you laugh,” said the director. “She’s a magic woman. She has that power.” Avilés described Sánchez as a natural fit for the role of Toña, a woman whose “quiet, nurturing presence serves as an intimate moral counterweight to the surrounding chaos.” “She’s a woman that hears, she’s a woman that sees, but most of all, she’s a woman that feels,” said the director. “She’s really connected to her students, to her vocation — her calling. She’s super enthusiastic. She wants to [create] a real transformation in her students.” Avilés’ third feature builds on her already formidable catalog, twice representing Mexico in the Oscar race for best international feature film. Creatively, she said, all three films exist on a continuum, with one project leading naturally to the next. “When I started to do ‘The Chambermaid,’ I already had ‘Totém’ in my heart. While I was doing ‘Totém,’ I knew I wanted to do ‘Cábula,’” she said. “Sometimes we have stories, and those stories go out [into the world]. It’s that persistence of stories that…are not in the mind, but in the heart.” A former actress who directed theater before venturing into filmmaking, Avilés has been praised as part of the new wave of female directors shaping Mexican cinema. title: Almodóvar’s Deep Dive Into … Almodóvar
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By David Canfield Plus Icon David Canfield Senior Entertainment Writer View All September 12, 2026 2:25am Pedro Almodóvar Courtesy of Getty Images Bitter Christmas is Pedro Almodóvar ’s 24th feature film over the course of 46 years. There’s never been more than a three-year gap between his releases. He won Cannes’ best director prize in the 1990s ( All About My Mother ), an Oscar for best screenplay in the 2000s ( Talk to Her ) and the Venice Film Festival’s top prize, the Golden Lion, just two years ago ( The Room Next Door ). With his latest movie, Bitter Christmas , the 76-year-old Spaniard remains on that restless trajectory, pushing himself deeper into uncharted territory — this time, by turning the camera back on himself. Related Stories Movies Sorry, Caleb Hearon Is Not Your Clown in 'Trash Mountain' Grief Dramedy Movies Courteney Cox Says She Decided to Direct 'Evil Genius' After Chance Encounter at the Beverly Hills Hotel: "I Made a Lot of Deals There" In fact, he does this within several sections of his cinematic nesting doll of a drama. The main plot follows Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia), a highly regarded filmmaker in the present day — and resembling Almodóvar in more ways than the spiked silver hair — writing a screenplay inspired by a period of his life from two decades earlier. Bitter Christmas shifts between Raúl’s day-to-day, centered on his real-life bonds with assistant Mónica (Aitana Sánchez-Gijón) and boyfriend Santi (Quim Gutiérrez) seeping into his fiction, and the evolving action of Raúl’s movie (also called Bitter Christmas — yes, we’re getting very meta here). That latter arc follows a director named Elsa (Bárbara Lennie) who begins suffering panic attacks while feeling out her relationship with her new boyfriend, a kindly stripper and firefighter named Bonifacio (Patrick Criado). Raúl ruminates over how much to pull from reality in telling Elsa’s story. At one point, he is confronted by a loved one about inserting a vulnerable, private moment from their life for his own script’s ending. He considers the overlap between Santi and Bonifacio. It can feel like you’re watching some sort of Almodóvar documentary — but of course, the director himself is the third layer. Raúl, too, is told through his lens. This made for an emotional process for Almodóvar, a master of melodrama who’s gone richly personal with modern classics like Bad Education and Pain and Glory . “This is a film in which I really expose myself a lot,” he says. “I have always been attracted to the very mysterious relationship between reality and creation. I didn’t want to pull back in being critical of myself and my own creative process.” Fans of Almodóvar can read into Bitter Christmas as much as they’d like — the lines between fact and fiction are blurry and ambiguous, and in conversation, Almodóvar shares key autobiographical reference points without diving into the specifics. Yet the introspection remains fascinating, especially for a director who’s never been afraid of big feelings rooted in aching truth. The dynamic between the ailing, short-tempered Elsa and the sweet, hunky Bonifacio is drawn directly from Almodóvar’s own relationship with a boyfriend from the early 2000s. (The director’s long-term partner is actor and photographer Fernando Iglesias.) “Migraines had accompanied me through a good chunk of my life, but the panic attacks were new to me, and this person, who I was only at the beginning of a relationship with, really saved me that first terrible weekend when it happened,” Almodóvar says. As Elsa’s story unfurls under the line-by-line command of Raúl’s typewriter, though, Bonifacio fades from that part of the narrative. There is deliberate “silence” here, as Almodóvar puts it: Is Bonifacio pining for Elsa? Frustrated with her being so preoccupied? Happy to wait for her return? The director will not say. “You don’t really know that much — like the relationship between Raúl and Santi,” he says. “You don’t know whether it’s a very joyful and shared physical partnership or whether one of them is much more in love than the other one. There’s not a lot of information that is shared.” Almodóvar is implicitly sharing here, of course, that he knows what he wants to hold back in interviews, too. What we don’t know of the characters, we don’t know of him. Bitter Christmas takes a thornier turn when Raúl, arguably, goes too far in his exploration of autofiction. This weds the film’s two timelines with a tensely electric current sourced all the way back to their creator. Almodóvar had to think about how far to push this line of storytelling — and perhaps, as a result, where he’d set his line for imagination to more explicitly take over. “It’s more of an ethical intuition than anything else because the genre of self-fiction doesn’t really set any limits, right?” he says. “The line for me is that I don’t want to harm the people that I use for inspiration. So far, I think I have succeeded. But when you’re dealing with reality and fiction, it’s always an ambiguous line — the limits are very porous.” Almodóvar reexamines this as we talk more, speaking frankly about how hard it can be for any subject, however loosely defined or camouflaged by remixed characteristics, to stay out of an artist’s way. “When an author is writing about the reality that is most proximate to them, you have to think that writers are always going to be selfish,” Almodóvar says later. “Once they have an idea for a story, they’re not necessarily going to think about who they are going to harm or not. Once you have that story, that inspiration, it’s quite powerful and valuable — as a writer, you don’t let it go.” That notion is clearly on Almodóvar’s brain these days. Bitter Christmas will make its North American premiere at the Toronto Film Festival on Sept. 13, before hitting select U.S. theaters on Nov. 13 — and so far, Almodóvar has been pleased to see audiences take the movie on its quirky terms. Meta-storytelling is in the air: We happen to be talking on the publication day for Life of M , Rachel Cusk’s novel widely alleged to center on a thinly veiled (and not always flattering) version of Natalie Portman. The reality is more complicated, certainly — Cusk has declined to comment on the rumors at all — but the media frenzy has already dominated the narrative around it. “This is one example in which using an inspiration perhaps did some harm,” Almodóvar says, eager to learn more about Cusk’s book. “It’s a danger of self-fiction — that it then just becomes gossip.” Almodóvar’s goal was the opposite: to look inward — to offer, for a filmmaker with a body of work as deep and accomplished as anyone of his generation, a rare and dishy window into how and why he does what he does. And maybe negotiate, in real time and for all to see, his dramaturgical boundaries. Indeed, above all, Bitter Christmas reveals Almodóvar’s profound, enduring love for making movies and why he’s not stopping anytime soon. “I’m invested in the force of the story, making sure that the story works, that the story interests people — the script is my focus,” he says. No matter the degree to which a movie like this becomes an exercise in veiled memoir, “It’s never with any kind of thought about my well-being. For me, the very fact of making films is the psychological support.” It’s no coincidence he’s begun to find a cinematic shape for these more cerebral ideas so much later in his career: “You lose the fear of exposing your intimacy,” he says. The result, inevitably, is one of Almodóvar’s bravest works — even as, or maybe because, it only raises more questions for the viewer along the way. THR

title: Gary Oldman Predicts HBO’s ‘Harry Potter’ Series Will Be ‘More Satisfying’ for Fans Than the Movies
full_text: Sep 11, 2026 10:54pm PT Gary Oldman Predicts HBO’s ‘Harry Potter’ Series Will Be ‘More Satisfying’ for Fans Than the Movies By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Gary Oldman Predicts HBO’s ‘Harry Potter’ Series Will Be ‘More Satisfying’ for Fans Than the Movies 6 hours ago Streaming Prices Continue to Balloon: Is ‘Streamflation’ at a Breaking Point? 17 hours ago Maria Bartiromo Says ‘More to Come’ in First Comments After Shock Fox News Exit: ‘I Am So Grateful for the Outpouring of Love’ 18 hours ago See All Getty Images Gary Oldman , who played Sirius Black in four “ Harry Potter ” movies, said he believes HBO’s forthcoming TV series adaptation set in the Wizarding World will be a bigger crowd-pleaser than the Warner Bros. films. That’s because the movies were significantly abridged from J.K. Rowling’s original books, whereas HBO’s “Harry Potter” is including far more of the source material, the British actor said in a recent interview with EW. Related Stories Bruno Dumont’s Cannes Movie 'Red Rocks' Sells to North America (EXCLUSIVE) Wim-Wenders Produced 'I'll Be Gone in June' Bought for North America After Cannes Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) “We had to cut a lot [for the ‘Harry Potter’ movies], and still we could only get the films down to, like, three hours,” Oldman said, adding that “a lot of character detail was sacrificed” in the process. “I believe [the HBO series is] gonna do it pretty much word-for-word, which I think, as a viewer, would be more satisfying.” Popular on Variety Oldman has previously opined that Sirius Black, a character he loves, did not get enough screen time in the movies . “He wasn’t in it enough. He turned up and then he went through the veil,” Oldman told IndieWire in 2024. Oldman’s Black first appeared in 2004’s “Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban,” but he had only cameos in “Goblet of Fire” and “Deathly Hallows Part 2″ and a brief appearance in “Order of the Phoenix” before his character is killed off. That said, Oldman told EW he is “proud” and “grateful” to have been part of the “Harry Potter” films “because it is such a phenomenon, the like of which I don’t think you’re ever gonna see again.” “When you think of that initial cast, someone in the story who doesn’t get a lot of credit anymore is [director] Chris Columbus, who set the world up and cast it,” he said. “We were extraordinarily lucky to have those people come back again, and again, and again, and literally grow into those roles.” Oldman will next appear in Season 6 of Apple TV’s “Slow Horses,” which premieres Sept. 16 . Season 1 of HBO’s “Harry Potter” TV show has wrapped and will premiere on HBO and HBO Max on Dec. 25. The second season, which will be based on the second book in Rowling’s beloved fantasy series, is currently in pre-production at Leavesden Studios outside London. HBO has not announced casting for the role of Sirius Black in the series to this point. The cast of HBO’s “Harry Potter” series includes Dominic McLaughlin in the title role alongside Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley; John Lithgow as Albus Dumbledore; Janet McTeer as Minerva McGonagall; Paapa Essiedu as Severus Snape; Nick Frost as Rubeus Hagrid; Rory Wilmot as Neville Longbottom; and Lox Pratt as Draco Malfoy. Meanwhile, Oldman once said that his performance as Sirius Black in the movies was “mediocre ,” but he later clarified that he didn’t mean to “disparage anyone out there who are fans of ‘Harry Potter’ and the films and the character who I think is much beloved.” “What I meant by that is, as any artist or any actor or painter, you are always hypercritical of your own work,” he told Variety in 2024. “If you’re not, and you’re satisfied with what you’re doing, that would be death to me. If I watched a performance of myself and thought, ‘My God, I’m fantastic in this,’ that would be a sad day.” Three Films, and a Second Oscar? title: Paramount Argues States’ Antitrust Suit Will ‘Collapse Under Scrutiny’
full_text: Sep 11, 2026 9:16pm PT Paramount Argues States’ Antitrust Suit Will ‘Collapse Under Scrutiny’ By Gene Maddaus Plus Icon Gene Maddaus Senior Media Writer @GeneMaddaus Latest Paramount Argues States’ Antitrust Suit Will ‘Collapse Under Scrutiny’ 8 hours ago Court to Hold Paramount-Warner Bros. Settlement Conference in Late October 17 hours ago Dan Schneider Loses ‘Quiet on Set’ Defamation Suit on Appeal 2 days ago See All Getty Images Paramount’s lawyers filed a legal response to the states’ antitrust lawsuit against the Warner Bros. Discovery merger on Friday, sketching out arguments and defenses it may use at a trial next March. Among other defenses, Paramount’s lawyers said they may claim that the coalition of 12 states lacks the authority to regulate the merger, “which is vested in the U.S. Department of Justice.” However, states do have the authority to bring claims alleging harms caused by conduct violative of federal antitrust law. Related Stories Bruno Dumont’s Cannes Movie 'Red Rocks' Sells to North America (EXCLUSIVE) Outsider Pictures Takes U.S. on Rafiki Fariala’s Award-Winning Cannes Hit 'Congo Boy' (EXCLUSIVE) Paramount also noted that Cinema United, the trade group for theater chains, has called for a settlement. Popular on Variety “Day by day, the weak case against this Merger gets even weaker,” the company argued, adding that it also plans to challenge the states’ market definitions. “Plaintiffs’ case amounts to a series of attempted shortcuts and assumptions that collapse under scrutiny.” California led the state coalition in suing to block the merger in July, arguing that the deal will create unlawful concentration in the basic cable market and in the wide-release and blockbuster theatrical markets. The DOJ had earlier approved the merger , issuing a memo laying out its reasoning for why the deal should be allowed to go forward. States typically work with the DOJ in antitrust cases, but under the Trump administration California and several others have often charted their own course. Paramount has repeatedly argued that the deal will be pro-competitive, and will result in more movies and TV shows. In its answer to the complaint , the company denied the states’ allegations — a requisite formality to establish a legal controversy. The company also added a few pages of argument, alleging that the states’ case ignores the broader context of an industry in rapid transition to streaming. “The way audiences consume content is changing rapidly. Streaming services now have greater viewership than movie theaters and cable television,” Paramount argues. “Plaintiffs’ case depends on ignoring this reality. It involves a series of gerrymandered markets based on cherry-picked data from the past. The alleged markets are not the product of sound economic analysis or current market realities. They have been invented for one purpose and one purpose only: to trigger a presumption — any presumption, no matter how weak — in the hopes the Court will look no further.” The Writers Guild of America has filed its own lawsuit arguing that the merger will reduce the marketplace for writers’ work. That case is set to be heard alongside the states’ challenge at trial on March 2, 2027. Paramount has agreed not to close the deal until a ruling is issued after the trial — though it is asking the court to require the plaintiffs to post a $1.88 billion bond as the price of continuing the litigation. A judge is set to hear arguments on that request on Sept. 24. Meanwhile, a court will hold a two-day settlement conference in the antitrust case with the parties in late October. That’s a standard part of civil procedure and does not indicate whether a deal is in the offing. title: Sorry, Caleb Hearon Is Not Your Clown in ‘Trash Mountain’ Grief Dramedy

So when the comic and actor co-wrote Trash Mountain with Ruby Caster, Hearon had to consider how much to lean into comedy as tears roll down his cheeks while starring alongside Zooey Deschenal in Kris Rey’s dramedy about love and grief. “No. If anything, I’m eager to prove that I’m not just a clown,” Hearon, the star of The Devil Wears Prada sequel and an HBO Max comedy special, told a Toronto Film Festival audience on Friday night after the world premiere of his comedic weepie. That led Hearon to break the tension by joking: “You stepped across a lot of lines. Once there, Gavin, who appears to have walked away from everyone he has ever loved in life, has an emotional reunion with his half-sister Abbi, played by Deschanel. “This was a really complicated guy, and he didn’t have a perfect son either,” Hearon said of his real-life father whose inspired character doesn’t appear onscreen in Trash Mountain . But the late father is ever-present as Gavin and Abbi pick through the detritus of his life and which grows in the front yard of his home as a mountain of rubbish to be hauled away. And as the siblings pick through mess their hoarder father left behind, one man’s trash becomes keepsakes that Gavin and Abbi must consider holding onto or leaving behind as junk. Deschanel decided after an early wardrobe call to bring one of the scarves her late grandfather wore before his death on set as a prop. “I have them in my closet, and every time I see them I think of my grandfather. These objects can be conduits for people that have passed,” Deschanel, best known for roles in All The Real Girls and The Good Girl, told the TIFF audience. Trash Mountain also stars Jackie Weaver, Jaboukie Young-White, Kyle Martin and Holmes, and Lilly Wachowski is among the executive producers. The Toronto Film Festival continues through to Sept. 20.
